summary:
Flame in Freefall – AI-Powered Fire and Combustion Analysis

Aero.Vision is an AI-powered research platform investigating fire behaviour, combustion, and flame dynamics in aerospace and microgravity environments.

Project Goal: To create an accessible, evidence-driven platform that brings together scientific research, AI-powered analysis, and data visualisation to better understand combustion in space and identify gaps in existing research.

Our platform features Ember, an interactive AI assistant with two modes:

Project Evidence Mode: Analyses curated research on experiments like Saffire-IV, FLEX, and BASS-II, providing source-linked answers and identifying evidence gaps.

General AI Mode: Answers broader scientific questions with automatic AI provider fallback.

Research Database: Organises experimental data on fuel properties, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and gravity.

Data Visualisation: Presents interactive charts for scientific analysis.

Evidence Gap Identification: Highlights areas requiring further research.

Interactive Dashboard: Offers chat history, intuitive navigation, and a floating AI assistant.

Aero.Vision addresses the challenge of understanding combustion under varying environmental conditions, supporting aerospace safety, fire prevention, and safer future space missions. It is important because reliable fire research is essential for aerospace safety, fire prevention, and the development of safer future space missions.
details:
Flame in Freefall – AI-Powered Fire and Combustion Analysis

Developed by Aero.Vision | AI Assistant: Ember

1. Project Overview and Objective

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific research and analysis platform developed to investigate combustion behaviour, flame dynamics, and fire safety in aerospace environments, particularly under microgravity conditions.

The central goal of our project is to make existing scientific research on combustion in space more accessible, organised, and understandable while identifying gaps in current experimental knowledge. Fire behaves differently in microgravity than it does under Earth's gravity, making conventional assumptions about flame behaviour and fire safety insufficient for certain space environments.

Our platform, Aero.Vision, addresses this challenge by integrating a structured scientific research database, AI-assisted investigation, interactive data visualisation, and evidence-based analysis into one unified dashboard.

2. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

Aero.Vision works as an integrated research environment with several interconnected modules.

A. Ember – AI Research Assistant

Ember is the platform's AI-powered assistant, designed with two specialised modes:

1. Project Evidence Mode

This mode focuses exclusively on our curated scientific research records. It analyses experimental information from studies such as NASA's Saffire-IV, FLEX, and BASS-II.

Its capabilities include:

  • Answering questions using available project research records.
  • Providing source-linked scientific information.
  • Identifying missing experimental parameters.
  • Distinguishing established findings from incomplete or uncertain evidence.
  • Highlighting research gaps instead of presenting unsupported conclusions.

A key restriction is that Ember must not invent experimental findings or treat missing information as proof of a scientific conclusion.

2. General AI Mode

This mode provides broader scientific explanations and answers questions beyond the curated research database. It uses external AI providers, with automatic fallback between Google Gemini and Groq if a provider encounters an error.

This ensures users can explore scientific concepts, ask follow-up questions, and understand complex combustion-related topics.

B. Scientific Research Database

We developed a structured database containing experimental records and relevant scientific parameters.

The database considers:

  • Fuel type and physical phase.
  • Sample shape and dimensions.
  • Oxygen availability and concentration.
  • Environmental pressure.
  • Airflow conditions.
  • Gravity conditions.
  • Experimental apparatus.
  • Sensors and measurement methods.
  • Evidence levels and original research sources.

This allows users to investigate how different environmental and experimental conditions relate to combustion behaviour.

C. Interactive Data Visualisation

The platform includes interactive charts that help users explore scientific information more effectively.

Features include:

  • Comparing oxygen and pressure conditions.
  • Exploring experimental records.
  • Comparing two research studies.
  • Examining relationships between recorded environmental parameters.

These visualisations transform structured experimental data into more understandable representations.

D. Evidence Gap Identification

One of the important features of Aero.Vision is its emphasis on identifying limitations in existing research.

Instead of assuming that all scientific parameters are available, the platform highlights missing measurements, incomplete records, and areas requiring further investigation.

It also distinguishes experimental observations from exploratory assessments, preventing preliminary interpretations from being mistaken for established scientific predictions.

E. Interactive Dashboard

The application is organised into dedicated sections:

  • Home: Introduces the project and its objectives.
  • Explore: Allows users to browse and filter research records.
  • Evidence: Presents scientific evidence and experimental sources.
  • Analyze: Provides interactive comparisons and visualisations.
  • Mission: Explores the relevance of research to aerospace environments.
  • About: Provides project and team information.

The interface also includes chat history, intuitive navigation, and a floating Ember assistant.

3. Benefits of the Project

Aero.Vision offers several advantages:

  1. Centralised Research: Brings multiple scientific experimental records into one organised platform.
  2. Evidence-Based Investigation: Encourages conclusions supported by actual research rather than assumptions.
  3. Time Efficiency: Makes it easier to locate, compare, and understand relevant scientific information.
  4. Scientific Transparency: Clearly identifies missing data and limitations in available evidence.
  5. Interactive Learning: Uses AI explanations and visualisations to make complex scientific concepts more accessible.
  6. Research Expansion: Helps identify questions that existing experiments may not have sufficiently addressed.

4. Intended Impact

The long-term intention of Flame in Freefall is to contribute to a better understanding of fire behaviour in environments beyond Earth.

As space exploration expands, fire safety becomes an increasingly important consideration aboard spacecraft, space stations, and future space habitats.

Our platform aims to support:

  • Improved understanding of combustion under microgravity conditions.
  • Research into spacecraft fire prevention and safety.
  • Identification of limitations in existing experimental research.
  • More accessible scientific investigation for students and researchers.
  • Future research into combustion under different environmental conditions.

The project is a research-support tool, not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system or a replacement for physical experiments.

5. Technologies, Programming Languages and Tools Used

We developed Aero.Vision primarily using Python and modern web technologies.

Programming language:

  • Python – Core application logic, data processing, AI integration, and backend functionality.

Framework and libraries:

  • Streamlit – Interactive web application and dashboard development.
  • Pandas – Scientific dataset organisation, processing, and analysis.
  • Plotly – Interactive charts and data visualisation.
  • Google GenAI SDK – Integration with Google Gemini.
  • Groq SDK – Integration with Groq AI services.
  • Streamlit Components – Additional interactive interface functionality.
  • Python libraries including pathlib, base64, re, and os – File handling, application utilities, and supporting functionality.

AI technologies:

  • Google Gemini – General AI assistance.
  • Groq – Alternative AI provider for automatic fallback.
  • Ember – Our integrated AI assistant with specialised research and general-purpose modes.

Data management:

  • CSV-based research datasets.
  • Structured experimental records and source references.
  • Separate catalogue and experimental-conditions datasets.

Development and deployment:

  • GitHub – Source-code management and version control.
  • Render – Cloud application hosting and deployment.
  • GoDaddy – Custom domain management.
  • Environment variables and deployment secrets – Secure API-key configuration.

Hardware:

The project was developed using a standard computer for programming, testing, and deployment. No specialised combustion apparatus or custom physical hardware was required to build the software platform.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of Flame in Freefall lies in combining scientific research, artificial intelligence, and interactive analysis into a single specialised platform.

Rather than developing another general-purpose chatbot, we designed Ember with two distinct operating modes to separate curated scientific evidence from broader AI-generated explanations.

Another important innovation is our emphasis on scientific limitations. Many digital research tools focus on presenting available information, whereas Aero.Vision also draws attention to what is missing, unverified, or insufficiently investigated.

The combination of a structured experimental database, source-linked AI responses, evidence-gap identification, and interactive comparisons creates a more responsible approach to AI-assisted scientific research.

We also designed the platform around a specific scientific challenge rather than simply integrating AI for general information retrieval.

7. Factors Considered During Development

Several scientific and technical considerations influenced our design:

Scientific factors:

  • Differences between terrestrial gravity and microgravity.
  • Fuel composition, physical state, and sample geometry.
  • Oxygen concentration and availability.
  • Environmental pressure and airflow.
  • Differences between experimental setups.
  • Reliability and completeness of scientific measurements.
  • Distinction between observed results and theoretical explanations.

Technical factors:

  • Accuracy and traceability of AI-generated responses.
  • Reliability of external AI providers.
  • Handling incomplete or unavailable research data.
  • Accessibility and ease of navigation.
  • Efficient organisation of scientific records.
  • Clarity of charts and experimental comparisons.
  • Secure management of API credentials.
  • Scalability and accessibility through cloud deployment.

We particularly prioritised preventing unsupported scientific claims. Missing experimental information is explicitly treated as an evidence limitation rather than an opportunity for the AI to guess.

8. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall represents our attempt to bring together aerospace research, artificial intelligence, and scientific data analysis to address an important challenge in future space exploration.

Through Aero.Vision and its AI assistant Ember, we have developed a platform that does more than retrieve information: it organises experimental evidence, facilitates comparisons, highlights research limitations, and makes complex scientific investigations more accessible.

Our ultimate vision is to support more informed research into combustion beyond Earth and contribute to the broader goal of making future space missions safer.
